title: The old Guru's voice
hook: Guru Amar Das wrote many hymns on ego, the Word and the mind
tomorrow: You are the form of light

segments.voice: Yesterday we closed Guru Angad's few, sharp lines. Your line was short and sharp. Did you write your one sharp line, and did it survive the day? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-two.

A page of the Guru Granth Sahib, and above the hymn, a small heading: Mahala three. The same signature in the verses, Nanak. But the voice has changed. Sikh tradition remembers Guru Amar Das as a man who came to the Guru late in life, who carried water before dawn for years, and who became Guru as an old man. Guru Angad's voice came in short verses. His successor's comes in hymns that keep circling three things: ego, the Word, and the mind. Today we start listening to that voice.
screen: `MAHALA THREE.` → `A LATE ARRIVAL, A LONG SERVICE.` → `EGO, THE WORD, THE MIND.`

segments.voice: Start with one line, from the Var in Raga Vadhans, paraphrased here: ego and the Name are opposed to each other; the two do not dwell in one place. That's the whole map in a sentence. Ego, in Punjabi haumai, is the feeling of I, I, mine, mine, the self at the center of every room. The Name, and the Word that carries it, is the Guru's teaching living in you. And the place where they can't live together is the mind, the man. It's like a small house with room for one guest. Ego has the room, or the Word has it. Both won't fit. Notice what he doesn't say. He doesn't say the mind is bad. He talks to it, again and again, the way you'd talk to someone you love who keeps wandering off. In the Anand, his song of bliss, he says, again paraphrased: O my mind, stay always with the Lord. That's not a scolding. It's a call home. And the way home, in his hymns, is the Word. Not willpower. Not cleverness. The Guru's Word, heard and sung and remembered, until it takes up the room where ego used to sprawl. Some readers hear in this the voice of a man who served for a long time before anyone called him Guru. He knows how ego dresses up, even inside service. He knows the mind doesn't settle because you tell it to once. So he says it more than once, and patiently. That patience is the old Guru's voice, and it's today's line.
screen: `TWO CANNOT LIVE IN ONE PLACE.` · `HAUMAI: I, I, MINE, MINE.` · `HE TALKS TO THE MIND, NOT AGAINST IT.` · `THE WORD TAKES UP THE ROOM.` · then, large: `THE OLD GURU'S VOICE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one of his hymns. If you have a gutka or a Gurbani app, find any hymn marked Mahala three, or the first verse of the Anand, and read it slowly, once. If you don't have one nearby, use the line from today: ego and the Name don't dwell in one place. Then, in the sit, let the breath slow and ask which of the three the words were speaking to: ego, the Word, or the mind. Keep that one in view, without needing to explain it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru quietly on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
The old Guru's voice. Guru Amar Das, heading Mahala three, patient and plain, speaking again and again of ego, the Word, and the mind. Today's word.
Your line: the old guru's voice. Once today, when the I, I, mine gets loud, hear his line under it: the two don't fit in one place. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-two.

screen: `DAY 1182 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: YOU ARE THE FORM OF LIGHT.`

howItsDone: Sikhs hear Guru Amar Das's hymns, headed Mahala 3, in kirtan at the gurdwara and in daily prayer: the Anand Sahib, which he composed, is part of the daily banis and is sung at the close of gatherings.

fork.setup: the mind keeps wandering after things, and ego fills every room. in his hymns, what brings the mind home?
options: the Guru's Word, heard and remembered.
leaving the house for the forest.
fork.reveal: in his hymns it's the Word: heard, sung and remembered until it takes the room where ego sprawled.

original.note: ego, the sense of I and mine; one of the subjects his hymns return to again and again.

trapdoor: what you thought: Guru Amar Das wrote about lots of separate topics.
what it means: ego, the Word and the mind are one story: one house, room for only one.
what a scholar hears: 'haumai navai naal virodh hai': ego and the Name are opposed (Vadhans ki Var, Mahala 3).
